title: EIS Page Viewer
text:
Helper Functions

def list_documents(project_id):
    """List all documents for a given project."""
    docs = eis_documents[eis_documents["project_id"] == project_id]
    if len(docs) == 0:
        print(f"No documents found for project_id: {project_id}")
        return None
    
    print(f"\nDocuments for project: {project_id}")
    print("-" * 80)
    display_cols = ["document_id", "document_type", "document_type_category", 
                    "main_document", "file_name", "total_pages"]
    available_cols = [c for c in display_cols if c in docs.columns]
    return docs[available_cols]


def view_page(document_id, page_num=1):
    """View a specific page from a document."""
    page = EIS_pages[(EIS_pages["document_id"] == document_id) & 
                    (EIS_pages["page_number"] == page_num)]
    
    if len(page) == 0:
        print(f"Page {page_num} not found for document_id: {document_id}")
        return None
    
    # Get document metadata
    doc = eis_documents[eis_documents["document_id"] == document_id]
    if len(doc) > 0:
        print(f"\n{'='*80}")
        print(f"Document: {doc.iloc[0].get('file_name', 'N/A')}")
        print(f"Type: {doc.iloc[0].get('document_type', 'N/A')} | "
              f"Category: {doc.iloc[0].get('document_type_category', 'N/A')} | "
              f"Main: {doc.iloc[0].get('main_document', 'N/A')}")
        print(f"{'='*80}")
    
    print(f"\n--- PAGE {page_num} ---\n")
    print(page.iloc[0]["page_text"])
    print(f"\n--- END PAGE {page_num} ---\n")
    return page.iloc[0]["page_text"]


def view_pages(document_id, start_page=1, end_page=5):
    """View a range of pages from a document."""
    # Get document metadata
    doc = eis_documents[eis_documents["document_id"] == document_id]
    if len(doc) > 0:
        print(f"\n{'='*80}")
        print(f"Document: {doc.iloc[0].get('file_name', 'N/A')}")
        print(f"Type: {doc.iloc[0].get('document_type', 'N/A')} | "
              f"Category: {doc.iloc[0].get('document_type_category', 'N/A')} | "
              f"Main: {doc.iloc[0].get('main_document', 'N/A')}")
        print(f"{'='*80}")
    
    for page_num in range(start_page, end_page + 1):
        page = EIS_pages[(EIS_pages["document_id"] == document_id) & 
                        (EIS_pages["page_number"] == page_num)]
        if len(page) > 0:
            print(f"\n--- PAGE {page_num} ---\n")
            print(page.iloc[0]["page_text"])
            print(f"\n--- END PAGE {page_num} ---\n")
        else:
            print(f"Page {page_num} not found")
            break


def view_project_pages(project_id, document_id=None):
    """View all pages of EISch document in a project (no truncation).
    
    Args:
        project_id: The project ID to filter documents
        document_id: Optional document ID to view only that specific document
    """
    docs = eis_documents[eis_documents["project_id"] == project_id]
    
    # Filter by document_id if provided
    if document_id is not None:
        docs = docs[docs["document_id"] == document_id]
        
    if len(docs) == 0:
        if document_id is not None:
            print(f"No document found with document_id: {document_id} in project_id: {project_id}")
        else:
            print(f"No documents found for project_id: {project_id}")
        return
        
    for _, doc in docs.iterrows():
        doc_id = doc["document_id"]
        print(f"\n{'='*80}")
        print(f"Document: {doc.get('file_name', 'N/A')}")
        print(
            f"Type: {doc.get('document_type', 'N/A')} | "
            f"Category: {doc.get('document_type_category', 'N/A')} | "
            f"Main: {doc.get('main_document', 'N/A')}"
        )
        print(f"{'='*80}")
                
        doc_pages = (
            EIS_pages[EIS_pages["document_id"] == doc_id]
            .sort_values("page_number")
        )
                
        for _, page in doc_pages.iterrows():
            print(f"\n--- PAGE {page['page_number']} ---\n")
            print(page["page_text"])


def search_pages(project_id, search_term):
    """Search for a term in all pages of a project."""
    docs = eis_documents[eis_documents["project_id"] == project_id]
    doc_ids = docs["document_id"].tolist()
    
    matching_pages = eis_pages[
        (eis_pages["document_id"].isin(doc_ids)) & 
        (eis_pages["page_text"].str.contains(search_term, case=False, na=False))
    ]
    
    print(f"\nFound {len(matching_pages)} pages containing '{search_term}'")
    print("-" * 80)
    
    for _, page in matching_pages.iterrows():
        doc = docs[docs["document_id"] == page["document_id"]].iloc[0]
        print(f"\nDocument: {doc.get('file_name', 'N/A')} | Page: {page['page_number']}")
        
        # Show context around the search term
        text = page["page_text"]
        idx = text.lower().find(search_term.lower())
        if idx >= 0:
            start = max(0, idx - 200)
            end = min(len(text), idx + len(search_term) + 200)
            context = text[start:end]
            if start > 0:
                context = "..." + context
            if end < len(text):
                context = context + "..."
            print(context)
    
    return matching_pages


def get_random_project(n_docs=2):
    """Get a random project with at lEISst n_docs documents."""
    import random
    doc_counts = eis_documents.groupby("project_id").size()
    eligible = doc_counts[doc_counts >= n_docs].index.tolist()
    
    project_id = random.choice(eligible)
    print(f"Random project with {doc_counts[project_id]} documents: {project_id}")
    return project_id

April 27, 2006

Mr. Scott Barker, Project Manager 
Bureau of Land Management 
15 East, 200 South 
Burley, ID  83318 
 
Dear Mr. Barker: 
 
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has reviewed the final Environmental Impact 
Statement (EIS) for the proposed Cotterel Wind Power Project and Resource Management Plan 
Amendment (CEQ No. 20060103) in Cassia County, Idaho.  The review was conducted in accordance with 
EPA responsibilities under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and Section 309 of the Clean Air 
Act (CAA).  This section of the CAA directs EPA to specifically review and comment in writing on the 
environmental impacts associated with all major federal actions.  Under our policies and procedures, we 
evaluate the document's adequacy in meeting NEPA requirements. 
 
The final EIS proposes construction, operation, and maintenance of a 190-240 megawatt (MW) 
wind-driven electric power generation facility on Cotterel Mountain, land primarily administered by the 
Bureau of Land Management (BLM); and amendments to the 1985 Cassia Resource Management Plan 
(RMP) to allow for the granting of a right-of-way (ROW) for development of the facility.  From four 
possible alternative actions proposed for the project, Alternative C has been identified as the final EIS 
preferred alternative.  Under this action, BLM would use fewer (81-98) but larger output (2-3 MW) wind 
turbines, construct 23 miles of roads (19.5 miles of new and 3.2 miles of reconstructed roads), build one 
substation, and set up 20 miles of new transmission interconnect lines.  Adverse impacts from the preferred 
Alternative C would be reduced using appropriate Best Management Practices (BMPs), effectiveness 
monitoring, adaptive management, and compensatory off-site mitigation. 
 
In our comments on the draft EIS in September 2005, EPA requested that the final EIS include 
information about the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) stormwater permit and 
recommended continued engagement of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Idaho Department of Fish and 
Game, and other experts on wind energy development issues throughout the life of the proposed project.  All 
changes made to the EIS between draft and final reflect the good work that BLM has done, working with 
interested stakeholders, and modifying the proposed action in response to public comments.  The responses 
provided in the final EIS address our concerns. 
 
EPA appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on the final EIS for this project. If you have 
questions about our comments, please contact Theogene Mbabaliye at (206) 553-6322. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
/S/ 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Christine B. Reichgott, Manager 
 
 
 
 
 
 
NEPA Review Unit

September 22, 2005

Mr. Scott Barker, Project Manager 
Bureau of Land Management 
15 East, 200 South 
Burley, ID  83318 
 
Dear Mr. Barker: 
 
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has reviewed the Draft Environmental 
Impact Statement (DEIS) for the proposed Cotterel Wind Power Project and Draft Resource 
Management Plan Amendment (CEQ No. 20050249) in Cassia County, Idaho.  The review 
was conducted in accordance with EPA responsibilities under the National Environmental Policy 
Act (NEPA) and Section 309 of the Clean Air Act (CAA).  This section of the CAA directs EPA 
to specifically review and comment in writing on the environmental impacts associated with all 
major federal actions.  Our review considers not only the impact to the environment but also the 
adequacy of the NEPA document itself. 
 
The DEIS analyzes the impact of a proposal to construct, operate and maintain a 190-240 
megawatt (MW) wind-driven electric power generation facility on Cotterel Mountain, land 
primarily administered by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM).  BLM will decide whether 
to grant a right-of-way (ROW) for the project and amend its 1985 Cassia Resource Management 
Plan (RMP). 
 
The DEIS analyzes four alternatives, A through D.  Alternative A is the no action 
alternative, under which the ROW would be denied.  Alternative B is the proposed action, with 
infrastructure that would include 130 turbines of 1.5 MW output each, 2 substations, 25 miles of 
roads (22.1 miles for new and 4.5 reconstructed roads), and a permanent project area of about 
203 acres.  The BLM’s preferred alternative is Alternative C, which is a modification of 
Alternative B using fewer (81-98) but larger output (2-3 MW) wind turbines, about 23 miles of 
roads (19.5 miles of new and 3.2 miles of reconstructed roads), 1 substation, and longer 
transmission lines (20 miles).  Alternative D would modify alternative C to avoid a portion of 
sage-grouse habitat using less overall acreage (158 acres) for the project and fewer wind turbines 
(66-82), 1 substation, and 17.4 miles of roads (14.5 miles of new and 2.9 of reconstructed roads).  
Both Alternatives C and D would include effectiveness monitoring, adaptive management, 
compensatory off-site mitigation, and a technical steering committee.  Alternatives B-D would 
require amendments to the Cassia RMP, which currently does not allow granting a ROW for 
wind energy development. 
 
 


--- PAGE 2 ---

2 
 
EPA supports development of alternative and environmentally sustainable sources of 
energy such as wind power.  The DEIS for this project includes a good analysis of the potential 
impacts of the Cotterel Mountain Wind Power Project.  We are particularly pleased that the 
interagency group of experts on wildlife biology (IWETT) and Technical Steering Committee 
are actively engaged as advisors on this project since wind power technology and configuration 
of wind turbines in this area are still relatively new.  Effective adaptive management will be 
important to minimize and mitigate impacts. 
 
The DEIS indicates that the primary impacts of this project are expected to be disruption 
of sage-grouse habitat and bird and bat mortality due to collisions with rotors.  Water quality 
may be adversely affected if construction alters the hydrology of springs and surface runoff such 
that erosion carries sediment to tributaries and ultimately to streams already listed on the 303(d) 
list for sediment and/or temperature.  The DEIS states that BMPs will be used to minimize these 
impacts.  We recommend that this aspect of the project be monitored to assure that water quality 
is protected.  A NPDES stormwater permit is required for construction projects that disturb more 
than one acre (40 CFR 122.26 (b)).  We recommend that the final EIS include information about 
this permit.  Air quality will be impacted in the short term due to construction activities and in 
the longer term due to traffic on unpaved roads, emissions from vehicles and on-site operations, 
and cumulative impacts from surrounding activities such as agriculture and fire.  Because the 
project site is within the Prevention of Significant Deterioration (PSD) Class II area, it will be 
important to monitor the situation and take corrective action if air quality standards are not met.  
We recommend that the BLM continue to work closely with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, 
Idaho Department of Fish and Game, and other experts on these issues throughout the life of the 
proposed project, particularly in effectiveness monitoring, adaptive management, and 
compensatory mitigation. 
 
We have assigned a rating of LO (Lack of Objections) to the DEIS.  This rating and a 
summary of our comments will be published in the Federal Register.  A copy of the rating 
system used in conducting our review is enclosed for your reference.   
 
Thank you for the opportunity to review this DEIS.  If you have questions or comments 
concerning this review, please contact Mr. Theogene Mbabaliye at (206) 553-6322 or by email at 
mbabaliye.theogene@epa.gov. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
/S/ Denise Clark for 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Christine B. Reichgott, Manager 
 
 
 
 
 
 
NEPA Review Unit

RECORD OF CATEGORICAL EXCLUSION DETERMINATION

A. Proposed Action: Western proposes to conduct pole replacement along the
existing Electrical District #2-Saguaro #1 115-kV transmission line. This will consist
of removing ninety-five (95) deteriorated wood poles by lifting or pulling them from
the ground, auger a 24" hole and installing new wood pole structures and associated
hardware. Western will use dozers, backhoes, front end loaders, dump trucks, trailer
trucks, water trucks, bucket trucks, crew trucks and pickup trucks to bring crews and
equipment to the project area. This work is necessary to maintain the safety and
reliability of the bulk electrical system.

The attached maps show the project areas are situated within Sections 30 & 31
Township 6 South Range 8 East, Sections 6, 7, 18, 19, 30 & 31 Township 7 South
Range 8 East, Sections 6, 7, 18, 19, 30 & 31 Township 8 South Range 8 East,
Sections 6, 7, 18, 19, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35 & 36 Township 9 South Range 8 East,
Sections 30, 31, 32 & 33 Township 9 South Range 9 East, Sections 3, 4, 10, 11 &
12 Township 10 South Range 9 East, Sections 7, 15, 16 & 17 Township 10 South
Range 10 East on the Gila and Salt River Meridian, Pinal County, Arizona. Work will
be conducted within Western's right of way. The corresponding U.S.G.S. 7.5-minute
topographic maps are Eloy North, Eloy South, Friendly Corners, Samaniego Hills &
Red Rock, Arizona. This work is planned to begin the month of November, 2011.

B. Categorical Exclusion Applied: 10 CFR, Part 1021, Subpart D, Appendix B, B1.3:
"Routine maintenance activities and custodial services for buildings, structures,
rights-of-way, infrastructures (e.g., pathways, roads, and railroads), vehicles and
equipment, and localized vegetation and pest control, during which operations may
be suspended and resumed. Custodial services are activities to preserve facility
appearance, working conditions, and sanitation, such as cleaning, window washing,
lawn mowing, trash collection, painting, and snow removal. Routine maintenance
activities, corrective (that is, repair), preventive, and predictive, are required to
maintain and preserve buildings, structures, infrastructures, and equipment
in a condition suitable for a facility to be used for its designated purpose. Routine
maintenance may result in replacement to the extent that replacement is in kind and
is not a substantial upgrade or improvement. In kind replacement includes
installation of new components to replace outmoded components if the replacement
does not result in a significant change in the expected useful life, design capacity, or
function of the facility. Routine maintenance does not include replacement of a major
component that significantly extends the originally intended useful life of a facility
(for example, it does not include the replacement of a reactor vessel near the end of
its useful life). Routine maintenance activities include, but are not limited to:...(m)
Repair and maintenance of transmission facilities, including replacement of
conductors of the same nominal voltage, poles, circuit breakers, transformers,
capacitors, crossarms, insulators, and downed transmission lines, in accordance,

2
where appropriate, with 40 CFR part 761 (Polychlorinated Biphenyls Manufacturing,
Processing, Distribution in Commerce, and Use Prohibitions)...."

C. Regulatory Requirements in 10 CFR 1021.410 (b):

1. The proposed action fits within a class of actions that is listed in Appendix B to
Subpart D.

a. The proposed action was reviewed for the requirements of the Endangered
Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the National
Historic Preservation Act, and all applicable Department of Energy Orders.

b. The proposed action does not require the siting, construction, or major
expansion of waste storage, disposal, recovery, or treatment facilities.

c. The proposed action does not disturb hazardous substances, pollutants,
contaminates, or CERLA-excluded petroleum and natural gas products that
pre-exist in the environment such that there would be uncontrolled and
unpermitted releases.

d. Should archaeological resources or vertebrate fossils be discovered during
implementation of the project all surface disturbing activities in the area of
discovery shall cease. An archaeologist will evaluate the discovery and
provide recommendations to the NEPA Compliance Officer. Surface
disturbing activities shall not resume in the area until permission is obtained
from the NEPA Compliance Officer.

2. There are no extraordinary circumstances related to the proposal that may affect
the significance of the environmental effects of the proposal; and

3. The proposal is not "connected" to other actions with potentially significant
impacts, is not related to other proposed actions with cumulatively significant
impacts, and is not precluded by 40 CFR 1506.1 or 10 CFR 1021.211.

D. Determination: Based on my review of information conveyed to me and in my
possession (or attached) concerning the proposed action, as NEPA Compliance
Officer (as authorized under DOE Order 451.1A), I have determined that the
proposed action fits within the specified class of actions, the other regulatory
requirements set forth above are met, and the proposed action is hereby
categorically excluded from further NEPA review.

3
E. Special Conditions:

1. An Archaeological monitor will be present during all construction activities.
Western will hold an onsite cultural awareness training session so that
construction personnel are aware of avoidance areas. The cultural monitor
will mark avoidance areas within the transmission line corridor near
structures, 13/1, 13/3, 18/4, 39/4, 39/5 & 44/5. The markings will be removed
at when ground disturbing activities in the area have been completed.

2. A Pre-Construction Biological Inspection of the project area will locate
areas to avoid. The qualified biologist will be responsible for overseeing
compliance with the avoidance and minimization measures for any desert
tortoise, Tucson shovel-nosed snake, or active bird nests located.

3. A Qualified Biologist will be present during all project activities that have
potential to disturb soil, vegetation, and wildlife in the desert shrubland
portions of the alignment. Western will hold an onsite biological awareness
training session so that construction personnel are aware of avoidance
areas.

4. The Biological Monitor will be authorized by Western to temporarily halt
construction activity if needed to prevent potential harm to Tucson shovel-
nosed snakes, desert tortoise, or nesting birds.

5. The work supervisor will coordinate with the Biological Monitor on planned
or ongoing activities in desert shrubland habitat and any specific
monitoring requirements for each activity in those areas.

6. If an active burrowing owl burrow is observed within the project area, the
Biological Monitor will designate and flag an appropriate buffer area
around the burrow where activities will not be permitted.

7. All trash and food items shall be properly contained within vehicles or
closed containers. The contents shall be regularly removed from the
project area to reduce the attractiveness of the area to ravens and other

8. No pets will be permitted on the work site.

9. All construction refuse will be removed from the site upon completion of

could be hazardous to vegetation or wildlife resources, shall be disposed

Decision
It is my decision to implement the Proposed Action, as described in DOI-BLM-CO-N010-2021-
0043-CX, authorizing the emergency repair of BLM Road 1509 in Moffat County, Colorado,
near the Little Snake/White River Field Office boundary. The repair is expected to consist of
layering compatible rock material and BLM-approved Geotech material, then installing a culvert
and armoring the inlet and outlet of the culvert with local rock material from a nearby rock pile,
within BLM standards. The road repairs are expected to be completed by a contractor using
standard road maintenance equipment (e.g., excavators, dozers, wheel loaders, and motor
graders), and is expected to be completed by August 2021.

The road repair is expected to take approximately one week to complete, with potential road
closure for one to two days if necessary. The repairs will require the removal of topsoil;
disturbance will be no more than three feet below grade. On-site material will be used where
possible, including native rock from a rock pile approximately one mile northeast of the failure
site (CX Appendix A, Figure 1). Construction activities will occur within 50 feet of the existing
road. Some road closures during construction are unavoidable but the BLM will communicate
these closures to the public in advance.

surface disturbance outside of the alluvial drainage channel.

Project Components and General Schedule
The project consists of layering compatible rock material and BLM-approved Geotech material,
then installing a culvert and armoring the inlet and outlet of the culvert with local rock material
from a nearby rock pile, within BLM standards. The road repairs are expected to take place by
August 2021.
Permanent road repairs would mostly likely be completed by a contractor.
The road repair would take approximately one week to complete, with potential road closure for
one to two days if necessary.
Permanent road repairs would be designed and implemented under the direction of a BLM
Engineer. The permanent road repairs essentially involve filling the road foundation with stable
materials such as large rock (riprap) and graded aggregates. To reduce costs, the BLM would
seek to use on-site material where possible, including native rock from a rock pile approximately
one mile northeast of the failure site (Appendix A, Figure 1). Construction activities would occur
within 50 feet of the existing road. Some road closures during construction are unavoidable but
the BLM would communicate these closures to the public in advance.
The permanent repairs would require the removal of topsoil; disturbance would be no more than
three feet below grade. Standard road maintenance equipment would be used (e.g., excavators,
dozers, wheel loaders, and motor graders).
Design Features
1. A cultural monitor shall be present for any activity with the potential to create new
surface disturbance outside of the alluvial drainage channel.
2. The following seed mix would be used for reclamation of any temporary re-route and any
other temporary construction disturbances after the permanent road repairs are
completed. Seeding would occur during the appropriate season to ensure seed
stratification (cold temperatures), germination, and establishment. Fall seeding is
recommended following project completion.

3. The BLM would develop an engineered construction/reclamation plan that includes:
a. How soil productivity would be maintained and restored;
b. Stormwater control measures and Best Management Practices (e.g., ditches,
catchments, energy dissipators, etc.) used to limit surface runoff and avoid
accelerated erosion such as rilling, gullying, piping, and mass wasting;
c. Roads and culverts designed and constructed according to the standards provided
in BLM Manuals 9112 and 9113 which would include:
i. Proper sized aggregate and riprap used during culvert construction.
ii. Energy dissipators at culvert outlets.
iii. Riprap at culvert entrance to streamline water flow and reduce erosion.
4. Collecting of nearby riprap material would not be allowed when soils are wet.
5. Surface collection (no excavation) of riprap material would only be allowed within 100
feet of the road.
6. Ground disturbance from riprap collection would be remediated upon removal.
7. Fueling of equipment would only occur on existing ground disturbance. Any spills would
be cleaned up immediately and disposed of properly.
8. The applicant is responsible for informing all persons who are associated with the project
that they would be subject to prosecution for knowingly disturbing archaeological sites or
for collecting artifacts.
9. If any archaeological materials are discovered as a result of operations under this
authorization, activity in the vicinity of the discovery would cease, and the BLM LSFO
Archaeologist would be notified immediately. Work may not resume at that location until
approved by the Authorized Officer (AO). The applicant would make every effort to
protect the site from further impacts including looting, erosion, or other human or natural
damage until BLM determines a treatment approach, and the treatment is completed.
Unless previously determined in treatment plans or agreements, BLM would evaluate the
cultural resources and, in consultation with the State Historic Preservation Office
(SHPO), select the appropriate mitigation option within 48 hours of the discovery. The
applicant, under guidance of the BLM, would implement the mitigation in a timely
manner. The process would be fully documented in reports, site forms, maps, drawings,
and photographs. The BLM would forward documentation to the SHPO for review and
concurrence.
10. Pursuant to 43 CFR 10.4(g), the applicant must notify the AO, by telephone and written
confirmation, immediately upon the discovery of human remains, funerary items, sacred
objects, or objects of cultural patrimony. Further, pursuant to 43 CFR 10.4(c) and (d), the
operator must stop activities in the vicinity of the discovery and protect it for 30 days or
until notified to proceed by the AO.
11. The applicant is responsible for informing all persons who are associated with the project
operations that they would be subject to prosecution for disturbing or collecting
vertebrate or other scientifically important fossils, collecting large amounts of petrified
DOI-BLM-CO-N050-2021-0043-CX
3
wood (over 25lbs./day, up to 250lbs./year), or collecting fossils for commercial purposes
on public lands.
12. If any paleontological resources are discovered as a result of operations under this
authorization, the applicant or any of his agents must stop work immediately at that site,
immediately contact the BLM Paleontology Coordinator, and make every effort to protect
the site from further impacts, including looting, erosion, or other human or natural
damage. Work may not resume at that location until approved by the AO. The BLM or
designated paleontologist would evaluate the discovery and take action to protect or
remove the resource within 10 working days. Within 10 days, the operator would be
allowed to continue construction through the site or would be given the choice of either
(a) following the Paleontology Coordinator's instructions for stabilizing the fossil
resource in place and avoiding further disturbance to the fossil resource, or (b) following
the Paleontology Coordinator's instructions for mitigating impacts to the fossil resource
prior to continuing construction through the project area.
Categorical Exclusion Review
The Proposed Action qualifies as a categorical exclusion under 516 DM 11.9, I1 for emergency
stabilization:
“Planned actions in response to wildfires, floods, weather events, earthquakes, or
landslips that threaten public health or safety, property, and/or natural and cultural
resources, and that are necessary to repair or improve lands unlikely to recover to a
management-approved condition as a result of the event. Such activities shall be limited
to: repair and installation of essential erosion control structures; replacement or repair
of existing culverts, roads, trails, fences, and minor facilities; construction of protection
fences; planting, seeding, and mulching; and removal of hazard trees, rocks, soil, and
other mobile debris from, on, or along roads, trails, campgrounds, and watercourses.
These activities:
a. Shall be completed within one year following the event;
b. Shall not include the use of herbicides or pesticides;
c. Shall not include the construction of new roads or other new permanent
infrastructure;
d. Shall not exceed 4,200 acres; and
e. May include temporary roads which are defined as roads authorized by
contract, permit, lease, other written authorization, or emergency operation not
intended to be part of the BLM transportation system and not necessary for long-
term resource management. Temporary roads shall be designed to standards
appropriate for the intended uses, considering safety, cost of transportation, and
impacts on land and resources; and
f. Shall require the treatment of temporary roads constructed or used so as to
permit the reestablishment by artificial or natural means, or vegetative cover on
the roadway and areas where the vegetative cover was disturbed by the
DOI-BLM-CO-N050-2021-0043-CX
4
construction or use of the road, as necessary to minimize erosion from the
disturbed area. Such treatment shall be designed to reestablish vegetative cover
as soon as practicable, but at least within 10 years after the termination of the
contract."
The Proposed Action has been reviewed with the list of extraordinary circumstances (43 CFR
46.215¹) described in the table below.

a) Have significant adverse effects on public health and safety.
b) Have significant impacts on such natural resources and unique geographic
characteristics as historic or cultural resources; park, recreation, or refuge lands;
wilderness areas; wild or scenic rivers; national natural landmarks; sole or
principal drinking water aquifers; prime farmlands; wetlands; floodplains;
national monuments; migratory birds; and other ecologically significant or critical
areas.
c) Have highly controversial environmental effects or involve unresolved
conflicts concerning alternative uses of available resources.
d) Have highly uncertain and potentially significant environmental effects or
involve unique or unknown environmental risks.
e) Establish a precedent for future action or represent a decision in principle about
future actions with potentially significant environmental effects.
g) Have significant impacts on properties listed, or eligible for listing, in the
National Register of Historic Places as determined by the bureau.
h) Have significant impacts on species listed, or proposed to be listed, on the List
of Endangered and Threatened Species, or have adverse effects on designated
Critical Habitat for these species.
i) Violate a Federal law, or a State, local or tribal law or requirement imposed for
the protection of the environment.
j) Have a disproportionately high and adverse effect on low income or minority
populations.
k) Limit access to and ceremonial use of Indian sacred sites on Federal lands by
Indian religious practitioners or significantly affect the physical integrity of such
sacred sites.
l) Contribute to the introduction, continued existence, or spread of noxious weeds
or non-native invasive species known to occur in the area or actions that may
promote the introduction, growth, or expansion of the range of such species.

Cultural Resources: The National Historic Preservation Act requires that federal land managing
agencies consider the effect of federal undertakings on historic and prehistoric sites that are
eligible to the National Register of Historic Places (NHRP). A review of existing records was
completed to determine the extent of previous cultural resource surveys and the location of
recorded sites in relation to the road repair and native rock pile locations. A small number (three:
MC.E.R12/21-85; MC.LM.R45/13-81; MF.LM.R249/10-94) of previous cultural inventories
occurred within a one-mile radius around the two locations; none of which intersected with the
proposed project areas. While cultural inventories in the area are limited, they did reveal
moderate site density around Sagebrush Draw; therefore, a Class III pedestrian survey was
warranted.
On May 8, 2021, BLM Colorado Northwest District archaeologist Wendy Parker surveyed a
total of 1.6 acres (0.8 acres at each location) around the road damage and rock pile locations. The
survey yielded negative results; therefore, the undertaking would have no effect on historic
properties and no further archaeological work is necessary.
Native American Religious Concerns: Lacking a written, formal agreement outlining a
consultation process between BLM-LSFO and the relevant tribes, the field office policy is to
consult with tribes when the proposed undertaking is within or in the vicinity of an area known
to be of concern to the tribes or when the undertaking involves sites of the kind that experience
has shown would be of tribal concern. Such sites include burials, rock art, wickiups, stone circle
sites, possible vision quest sites, possible eagle traps, etc. As the road damage and rock
procurement area is not in or near an area of known concern to the tribes, nor would it be in the
vicinity of sites of the kind that are of tribal concern, it is concluded that proposed undertaking
would not affect areas or sites of Native American concern.

Two tabs: - Programmatic (16 projects): Reviews that ARE programmatic EIS/EAs - Tiered (10 projects): Reviews that tier FROM a programmatic review
Key columns for reviewers: - evidence_text — text that triggered classification - tiers_from — (tiered only) programmatic review being referenced - correct — Yes/No/Unsure - notes — comments




Duplicates: Some projects have same title but different project_id — need manual review
Missing project: 3621210fbd086bddbbf6fbedc1d6a488 has “programmatic” in file name but was classified as “standard” — may need file name search added to extraction

Problem: Programmatic/tiered reviews are very rare. - Only 26 found out of 1,416 projects (1.8%) - Tiered reviews (10) fewer than expected (estimated 5-15%)

Programmatic EIS/EA: A broad environmental review that analyzes a class of similar actions (e.g., all solar projects on BLM land). These serve as “umbrella” documents.
Examples found: - “Programmatic Environmental Assessment for System-wide Operations and Maintenance” - “Recycle of Scrap Metal Originating From Radiological Areas” (THIS PROGRAMMATIC ENVIRONMENTAL…)



Tiered Reviews: Project-specific reviews that reference and build upon a programmatic review. They don’t repeat analysis already done, potentially making them faster.
Examples found: - “This EA tiers from the 2012 NPR-A IAP/EIS and its ROD” - “The EA tiered from the analysis conducted in [programmatic review]”

title: Generation Capacity Workflow Status
text:
Date: 2026-01-30


Capture the current state of generation-capacity extraction work for Deliverable 3, summarize key findings on transmission/utilities prevalence in clean energy projects, and provide a runbook for rerunning the workflow.




Title-first extraction: scan project_title before documents; if a capacity is found, mark the project as done and skip document scanning.
Power vs energy split: power (MW/GW/kW) is tracked separately from energy (MWh/GWh/kWh) with new fields.
Expanded unit patterns: MWac/MWdc/MWe/MWt/MWth/MWp, kWe, and hyphenated forms; also handles ranges and “up to” expressions.
Invalid match filtering: filters MW-year and $/MW style matches.
Confidence fields added: project_gencap_confidence (high/medium/low) and project_gencap_context (local snippet).
Transmission-only gating has been removed; transmission-only projects are included in the regex pass.
LLM model default set to llama3.2:3b-instruct-q4_K_M.
LLM pass restricted to low/medium confidence cases by default and can run in parallel.
LLM hardening: requires numeric source quotes, rejects no-numeric candidates, and falls back to extracting the max numeric capacity from candidate sentences when the LLM omits a quote (marks extraction_method = fallback_from_candidates).
LLM can now be constrained to projects that already have regex capacity (--require-regex-capacity).
Regex extraction now skips likely initials/date false positives (e.g., “MW, 5/21/15”).
Added merge script to combine regex + LLM outputs into a single dataset.
Added lightweight validation flags and audit sample generator for regex capacities (initials/date, non-generation context, non-build context, equipment lists).
Stratified validation sample script added.




Clean energy projects: 22,279 total.
Overall: - Any “Electricity Transmission” in project_type: 7,815 (35.1%) - Transmission-only (strict: only Electricity Transmission + Utilities): 1,531 (6.9%) - Transmission-only (relaxed: also allow Broadband): 1,784 (8.0%) - Utilities-only (only Utilities, no transmission): 488 (2.2%)
By dataset source (percent of clean energy in each source): - CE: any transmission 34.3%, transmission-only strict 7.0%, relaxed 8.0%, utilities-only 2.3% - EA: any transmission 43.2%, transmission-only strict 5.6%, relaxed 6.1%, utilities-only 1.6% - EIS: any transmission 49.1%, transmission-only strict 1.5%, relaxed 2.0%, utilities-only 0.6%




Sample file created: output/deliverable3/gencap_manual_validation_sample.csv
20 clean-energy projects with non-null extracted capacity were sampled.
11/20 have a text snippet captured (match found within first 10 pages of the main doc). The remaining 9 are marked N/A for manual verification due to missing snippets.
Baseline precision on verifiable rows: 11/11 = 100% (limited to rows with snippets).
Main uncertainty noted: whether some matches clearly refer to the proposed project vs. another project (several notes flagged this).





10-project CE sample restricted to regex-capacity cases resulted in 9/10 capacity extractions (90%).
Methods: 5 llm, 4 fallback_from_candidates, 1 no_candidates.
The only miss was a false-positive regex match (initials/date “MW”).
Example fix: Barr‑Tech case now returns 2.2 MW via fallback.




Transmission-only gating has been removed. All projects, including transmission-only, are scanned by the regex pipeline.



data/analysis/projects_gencap.parquet now includes: - project_gencap_value, project_gencap_unit (power only) - project_gencap_energy_value, project_gencap_energy_unit (energy only) - project_gencap_source (title/document/none/skipped_transmission_only) - project_gencap_confidence (high/medium/low) - project_gencap_context (local text snippet)

This runs CE/EA/EIS in parallel and automatically combines to: data/analysis/projects_gencap.parquet.

df = pd.read_parquet("data/analysis/projects_gencap.parquet")

title: Energy Classification Filtering Logic
text:
This document summarizes all filtering iterations used to classify projects as “Clean”, “Fossil”, or “Other” energy types.


The energy classification pipeline applies multiple filtering layers to ensure accurate categorization. Projects initially classified as “Clean” may be reclassified to “Other” if they match exclusion criteria.




Location: code/extract/classify_energy.py → is_utilities_to_filter_out()
Criteria: Projects are excluded from “Clean” if they have ONLY: - “Utilities (electricity, gas, telecommunications)” tag - PLUS one of these non-energy tags (and no other tags): - Broadband - Waste Management - Land Development - Housing - Land Development - Other - Land Development - Urban
Rationale: These are likely telecommunications infrastructure or development projects with utility connections, not clean energy production projects.




Location: code/extract/extract_data.py → load_military_project_ids()
Criteria: Projects with BOTH: - “Military and Defense” project_type tag - “Nuclear” project_type tag
Source: Project IDs loaded from notes/military_project_ids_to_filter.csv
Rationale: Defense-related nuclear projects (weapons programs, naval reactors) are not civilian clean energy.
Note: The CSV is generated by running the exploratory section in code/deliverable1/02_agency.R.




Location: code/extract/extract_data.py → apply_energy_type_filters()
Criteria: Projects are excluded from “Clean” if they have BOTH: - “Waste Management” project_type tag - “Nuclear” project_type tag
AND are associated with one of these DOE offices (checked in lead_agency, project_sponsor, OR project_title), unless a keep list is present (see override below).



National Nuclear Security Administration, NNSA
Kansas City Field Office / National Security Campus
Livermore Field Office / Site Office, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
Los Alamos (Field Office, Site Office, Area Office, National Laboratory)
Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program / Laboratory
Nevada Field Office / National Security Site
Pantex Field Office / Plant
Sandia Site Office / Field Office / National Laboratories
Savannah River (Mission Completion, Operations Office, Field Office, Site)
Y-12 Site Office / Field Office / National Security Complex





Office of Legacy Management
Legacy Management
Albuquerque Operations Office
Grand Junction Office





Office of Environmental Management
Environmental Management
Hanford Site, Hanford Mission Integration Solutions
Richland, Richland Operations Office
Office of River Protection
Paducah, Paducah Site
Portsmouth, Portsmouth Site, Portsmouth and Paducah Field Office
Oak Ridge, Oak Ridge Office of Environmental Management
Waste Isolation Pilot Plant (WIPP)
Carlsbad, Carlsbad Field Office

Source (default): Exclusion terms loaded from notes/agencies_to_be_excluded.txt Override (keep list present): If notes/nuclear_waste_projects_to_keep.csv exists, then all Nuclear + Waste Management projects are excluded except those in the keep list, which were determined by CAFT to be project relevant.
Rationale: Nuclear waste cleanup, storage, and legacy site management are not clean energy production.
Note: The keep list represents client-reviewed exceptions and is authoritative when present. This switches the filter to a tag-based rule for Nuclear + Waste, reclassifying all others to “Other.” Clean energy count reduced by ~1,554 (from ~22,279 to ~20,725).





Location: Same as Filter 3, extended to check project_title Applies: Only when the keep list is not present (default mode)
Criteria: Same as Filter 3, but also checks project_title field for exclusion terms.
Rationale: Some projects had missing or incomplete project_sponsor fields, causing them to slip through the original filter. For example, “Hanford Site” might appear only in the title. This catches such cases.
Impact: Captured ~84 additional projects that were previously misclassified.





Order of operations: Filters are applied after initial energy classification in classify_energy.py, during the apply_energy_type_filters() step.
Affected columns:

project_energy_type - Updated from “Clean” to “Other”
project_energy_type_strict - Updated from “Clean” to “Other”

Flag columns added:

project_is_military_nuclear - Boolean
project_is_nuclear_waste - Boolean
project_utilities_to_filter_out - Boolean (in classify_energy.py)

File dependencies:

notes/agencies_to_be_excluded.txt - Exclusion terms (editable)
notes/military_project_ids_to_filter.csv - Military project IDs (generated by R)
notes/nuclear_waste_projects_to_keep.csv - Keep list (client-reviewed)






To add new exclusion terms: 1. Edit notes/agencies_to_be_excluded.txt 2. Add terms under the appropriate section (NNSA, LM, or EM) 3. Re-run python code/extract/extract_data.py --mode analysis
To regenerate military project IDs: 1. Run the exploratory section in code/deliverable1/02_agency.R 2. This writes to notes/military_project_ids_to_filter.csv

text:
This notebook helps you: 1. See real examples of capacity mentions in documents 2. Understand which document types contain capacity info 3. Test different extraction approaches
import pandas as pd
import re
from pathlib import Path
from collections import Counter

# Paths

def find_capacity_sentences_for_project(project_id, docs_df, pages_path, max_pages=20):
    """Find capacity-related sentences for a project."""
    # Get project's documents
    project_docs = docs_df[docs_df['project_id'] == project_id]
    if project_docs.empty:
        return []
    
    # Prioritize main documents
    main_docs = project_docs[project_docs['main_document'] == 'YES']
    if main_docs.empty:
        main_docs = project_docs
    
    # Get first main document
    doc_id = main_docs.iloc[0]['document_id']
    
    # Load pages
    try:
        pages_table = pq.read_table(pages_path, filters=[('document_id', '=', doc_id)])
        doc_pages = pages_table.to_pandas()
    except:
        return []
    
    # Search first N pages
    findings = []
    for _, page in doc_pages.head(max_pages).iterrows():
        candidates = extract_candidate_sentences(page['page_text'])
        for sent in candidates:
            if re.search(r'\d+\s*(?:MW|GW|kW|megawatt|gigawatt)', sent, re.IGNORECASE):
                findings.append({
                    'page': page['page_number'],
                    'sentence': sent[:400]
                })
    
    return findings

section: 8. Example: What LLM Input Would Look Like
text:
8. Example: What LLM Input Would Look Like
If we send candidate sentences to an LLM, here’s what the input/output would be.

# Example LLM prompt construction
def build_llm_prompt(sentences, project_title):
    """Build a prompt for LLM extraction."""
    prompt = f"""Extract the proposed project's generation capacity from the following text excerpts.

Project: {project_title}

Return JSON with this structure:
{{
    "capacity_value": <number or null>,
    "capacity_unit": "MW" | "GW" | "kW" | null,
    "confidence": "high" | "medium" | "low",
    "source_quote": "<exact quote from text>"
}}

Rules:
- Extract the PRIMARY project capacity, not alternatives or comparisons
- If multiple values exist, prefer "nameplate" or "rated" capacity
- If text mentions a range (e.g., "50-100 MW"), use the higher value
- Return null values if no clear project capacity is stated

Text excerpts:
"""
    for i, sent in enumerate(sentences[:5]):  # Limit to 5 sentences
        prompt += f"\n[{i+1}] {sent}\n"
    
    return prompt

# Show example
if len(capacity_findings) > 0:

Executive Summary






Key Findings




Multi-state projects represent a subset of clean energy projects that span state boundaries, often involving transmission lines or large-scale renewable energy connections
Multi-department projects are relatively rare but involve coordination between multiple federal departments
Multi-department projects are only Categorical Exclusions (CE): Among clean energy projects, all 21 multi-department projects are CEs; no EA or EIS projects have multiple lead agencies
Geographic patterns reveal regional clusters of interstate cooperation



This report aims to create the following set of deliverables:

Data on geography/project location; whether projects are multi-state or multi-agency

It analyzes clean energy projects that cross administrative boundaries—either spanning multiple states or involving multiple federal agencies. These projects often represent larger, more complex undertakings that require coordination across jurisdictions. title: AI Cost Estimates for Phase 2 Document Reading
text:
Phase 2 deliverable (concept note)
Benefit from AI document reading to create variables?
Why




Data analysis and visualizations
Yes
AI can extract structured variables from NEPA documents at scale to support analysis and visualization.


Draft and final report
Yes (indirect)
Report depends on derived variables; AI-assisted extraction accelerates synthesis.


Fact sheet
Yes (indirect)
Fact sheets summarize findings from the analysis; AI-derived variables improve coverage.


Supplemental technical report
Yes
Technical report can document AI-derived variable definitions, extraction methods, and validation.

title: AI Cost Estimates for Phase 2 Document Reading
text:
Phase 2 analysis topic
AI document reading needed?
Notes




Reasons why NEPA was triggered (e.g., federal land, federal funding)
Likely
Often described in project docs; AI can classify trigger reasons.


Determinations of significance across resource areas; factors contributing to significant impact
Yes
Requires text extraction from findings and impact discussions.


Mitigated FONSIs
Yes
Identifying mitigation and FONSI context is document-text heavy.


Differences/similarities between NEPA reviews for fossil vs clean energy (CEs, timelines, geography, etc.)
Partial
Some variables in metadata; others require reading project narratives.


Differences in analysis of visual impacts between clean energy and fossil projects
Yes
Requires detecting visual/aesthetic impact language in text.


Timelines for CEs, EAs, EISs (segmented by year, CEQ regs, agency, project type)
Partial
Dates often in metadata; some may require text or NOI cross-references.


Timeline outliers and case studies (whether NEPA was a cause of delay)
Likely
Requires qualitative interpretation from documents.


Cross-reference NOI in Federal Register for start date
No (API/metadata)
Better handled via structured API, not LLM reading.


Technical support for new regulatory CEs: identifying patterns in FONSIs
Yes
Pattern discovery from FONSI text benefits from AI extraction.

title: Phase 2 Deliverable Assessment
text:
Date: 2026-02-11



Before diving into each deliverable, the overarching lessons from Phase 1 are critical:

Messy, unstructured data is the constant enemy. Metadata is sparse, text formats are inconsistent across agencies, and even “simple” extraction tasks (like finding a decision date with a signature block) required multi-iteration pipeline development (regex -> hybrid LLM -> BERT -> 11+ refinements).
Initiation-style tasks (finding implicit information) are far harder than decision-style tasks (finding explicit information). BERT decision coverage hit 85%, but initiation stalled at 16% – and that gap persists despite extensive pattern expansion and class rebalancing. Phase 2 deliverables lean heavily toward the “initiation” end of this spectrum (implicit, contextual, requires reasoning).
Local LLMs (Llama 3.2 3B) work for classification but struggle with comprehension. The hybrid timeline approach showed this clearly: the LLM can label “is this a decision date?” but it can’t reliably reason about why a project triggered NEPA or what constitutes significant impact.
Every extraction task took 2-3x the initially estimated time once you factor in validation, false positive triage, class imbalance, and re-runs.







Difficulty: MODERATE-HIGH
What it requires: For each project, identify why NEPA was triggered – federal land, federal funding, federal permits, or some combination. This means reading project documents and classifying the federal nexus.
What works in your favor: - The lead agency is already in the metadata and is often a strong proxy (BLM -> federal land; DOE -> federal funding). You could get 60-70% coverage from metadata-based heuristics alone before touching document text. - The “trigger” language is sometimes explicit: “This EA is prepared because the proposed action involves a federal lease on BLM-managed land.” - Regex can catch many explicit patterns.
Problems I foresee: - Many documents don’t explicitly state why NEPA was triggered – the federal nexus is assumed by context. A CE for a cell tower on National Forest land doesn’t say “because it’s on federal land”; it just says “Coldfoot Cell Tower, Tongass National Forest.” - Distinguishing “mentioned” from “triggered by” is hard. A project might discuss federal funding in one section but the actual trigger is federal land use. - Multiple triggers per project is common and ambiguous. - 445K targeted pages is large. Even with 30% prefiltering, you’re sending ~134K pages to an LLM. - A local 3B model likely can’t do this well. This is a comprehension/inference task, not just pattern matching.
Realistic time estimate: 35-50 hours
High-level plan:

Build a metadata-based heuristic classifier (agency -> trigger type mapping) – covers the easy cases (~60-70%) (5 hrs)
Develop regex patterns for explicit trigger language (“federal land,” “DOE funding,” “Section 404 permit,” etc.) (5 hrs)
Run regex extraction on the full corpus with prefiltering (3 hrs)
For ambiguous/missing cases, design an LLM prompt and test on a 50-project sample – evaluate whether Llama 3B is sufficient or you need an enterprise model (8 hrs)
Full LLM run on remaining unresolved cases (5 hrs)
Manual validation on a stratified sample of ~50-100 projects (5 hrs)
Iterate on false positives/negatives, re-run (5-10 hrs)
Analysis & visualization (4 hrs)





Difficulty: HIGH – This is the hardest deliverable and the highest risk
What it requires: For FEIS/DEIS documents, extract which resource areas (air quality, water, wildlife, cultural resources, etc.) were found to have “significant impacts.” Then, starting with mitigated FONSIs, identify cases where impacts would have been significant but were mitigated.
What works in your favor: - EIS documents are relatively structured – they typically have chapters organized by resource area (Chapter 3: Affected Environment, Chapter 4: Environmental Consequences). - The vocabulary of significance is somewhat formulaic (“significant adverse impact,” “less than significant with mitigation,” etc.). - Only ~371K pages from FEIS/DEIS documents, which is a smaller subset.
Problems I foresee – and they are serious: - No standard format across agencies. DOI, DOE, USDA, DOD all structure their impact analyses differently. Some use tables, some use narrative, some use a hybrid. Section numbering varies. - Significance language is highly nuanced. “The proposed action would result in significant impacts to…” vs. “The proposed action would not result in significant impacts to…” – these differ by one word. Worse, many documents use hedging: “potentially significant,” “significant but mitigable,” “significant and unavoidable.” - Mitigated FONSIs are exceptionally tricky. You need to identify that (a) an EA found potentially significant impacts, AND (b) mitigation measures reduced them below significance, AND (c) the FONSI was issued with conditions. This is a multi-step reasoning chain. - A 3B local model will almost certainly fail at this task. This requires reading comprehension, not pattern matching. The distinction between “significant” and “not significant” in environmental documents is exactly the kind of nuanced language understanding that requires a large model. - Resource area segmentation adds another dimension – you’re not just classifying significance for the whole document, but for ~10-15 different resource areas per document.
Realistic time estimate: 55-75 hours
This is where I’d most strongly recommend budgeting for enterprise LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet). The $115 estimate in the proposal assumes cost-efficient mini models with 30% prefiltering – but the accuracy of a mini model on this task will likely be poor, and you may need the full-capability model. At GPT-4o pricing, 371K pages could run $300-500+ depending on context length.
High-level plan:

Define the taxonomy of resource areas and significance levels (with client input) (3 hrs)
Identify the structural patterns of EIS chapters across the top 5-6 agencies – map how they organize resource area analysis (6 hrs)
Build a document structure parser that identifies relevant sections/chapters (avoiding appendices, references, etc.) (8 hrs)
Design the LLM extraction prompt – test on 20 FEIS documents with both a local model and an enterprise model, compare accuracy (8 hrs)
Decision point: If local model accuracy is <70%, switch to enterprise LLM (likely outcome)
Full extraction run with enterprise LLM, focusing on identified relevant sections (6 hrs)
Mitigated FONSI sub-pipeline: identify FONSIs with mitigation conditions, extract the resource areas and mitigation types (10 hrs additional – this is essentially a second extraction task)
Validation on a stratified sample (5 hrs)
Analysis & visualization (5 hrs)





Difficulty: MODERATE
What it requires: Compare fossil fuel vs. clean energy and linear vs. non-linear project reviews across CE/EA/EIS rates, timelines, geography, and other dimensions.
What works in your favor: - This is primarily an analytical/comparative deliverable, not an extraction one. Most of the underlying data already exists from Phase 1. - The energy type classification is already built (clean/fossil/other). - Linear vs. non-linear can be derived from existing project type tags (transmission, pipelines = linear; generation = non-linear). - The 788K page count in the proposal seems high – this may be for validation or supplementary extraction, but the core analysis uses already-extracted data.
Problems I foresee: - Depends heavily on timeline quality. If initiation coverage remains at 16%, the timeline comparisons between fossil fuel and clean energy will be based on incomplete data. Duration statistics could be misleading. - Sample sizes for some categories may be small. Fossil fuel EIS projects vs. clean energy EIS projects – are there enough of each for meaningful comparison? - The “visual impacts” mention in the proposal is vague and could turn into a significant extraction task if it means actually identifying visual impact discussions in documents.
Realistic time estimate: 30-40 hours
High-level plan:

Create the linear/non-linear classification from existing project types (3 hrs)
Merge all Phase 1 + Phase 2 extracted datasets (timelines, capacity, reviews, geography) (4 hrs)
Build comparison tables: CE/EA/EIS rates by fossil vs. clean, linear vs. non-linear (5 hrs)
Timeline comparison analysis (duration by energy type, project type) – depends on D4 timeline quality (6 hrs)
Geographic analysis: where do fossil vs. clean energy reviews happen? (4 hrs)
Statistical testing and visualization (6 hrs)
Write-up and narrative (5 hrs)





Difficulty: MODERATE-HIGH
What it requires: Extend the Phase 1 BERT timeline pipeline to categorical exclusions (CEs), cross-reference Federal Register NOIs, and perform segmentation/outlier analysis.
What works in your favor: - The BERT pipeline infrastructure is built and battle-tested. - Decision coverage is decent at 85%. - Federal Register linking code already exists (code/extract/federal_register.py, data/analysis/noi_federal_register.parquet). - The segmentation analysis (pre/post-FRA, by agency, by year) is straightforward once timelines exist.
Problems I foresee: - CE documents are fundamentally different from EA/EIS documents. They’re often 1-3 page forms, sometimes with checkbox dates, sometimes with no narrative at all. The current regex/BERT approach was tuned for EA/EIS-style documents with signature blocks and narrative text. CE forms may need a different extraction approach entirely. - Initiation remains the Achilles’ heel. At 16% coverage, you can’t compute meaningful durations for most projects. The Phase 1 experience suggests this won’t improve dramatically without manual labeling or fundamentally different data sources (like Federal Register NOIs). - Federal Register NOI matching is fuzzy. Matching a NEPATEC project to its corresponding Federal Register NOI requires name/agency/date matching, which is error-prone. - CE projects are the vast majority (~20K of ~22K clean energy projects) but many may have trivially short timelines, skewing any aggregate analysis.
Realistic time estimate: 30-45 hours
High-level plan:

Analyze a sample of 50 CE documents to understand their structure and date patterns – determine if BERT approach transfers or needs adaptation (5 hrs)
If CE forms need new patterns: expand regex patterns, regenerate training data, retrain BERT (8 hrs)
Run BERT on full CE corpus (1-2 hrs compute time)
Federal Register NOI cross-referencing: improve fuzzy matching, validate on sample (6 hrs)
Use NOI dates as initiation fallback where BERT initiation is missing (3 hrs)
Segmentation analysis: pre/post-FRA, by agency, by project type, by year (5 hrs)
Outlier identification and case study selection (4 hrs)
Visualization (3 hrs)





Difficulty: MODERATE (but open-ended)
What it requires: Cluster FONSI documents by project type and mitigation measures to identify patterns that could support new categorical exclusion (CE) development.
What works in your favor: - Only 5,760 pages – orders of magnitude smaller than other deliverables. - FONSIs are relatively short, structured documents. - Modern embedding models (even local ones) can produce good document representations for clustering. - The client has a clear use case (supporting regulatory CE development), which gives the analysis a target.
Problems I foresee: - “Patterns” is vague. What constitutes a useful pattern for CE development? This needs careful scoping with the client. Are you looking for: project types that routinely get FONSIs (suggesting they could be CEs)? Common mitigation conditions? Resource areas that consistently come up? - Mitigation measure extraction is itself an NLP task. Mitigation conditions vary from “The project shall install erosion control barriers” to “The applicant agrees to the following 47 conditions…” – extracting and categorizing these could be a full pipeline. - Clustering can produce garbage. If the document features aren’t well-chosen, you’ll get clusters that don’t mean anything actionable.
Realistic time estimate: 18-30 hours (depends on how deep the client wants to go)
High-level plan:

Scope with client: define what “patterns” means for CE development – what would an actionable finding look like? (2 hrs)
Extract FONSI document text, filter to main document body (3 hrs)
Generate document embeddings (can start with local sentence-transformers model) (2 hrs)
Cluster analysis: try topic modeling (LDA) and embedding-based clustering (k-means on embeddings) (4 hrs)
Identify cluster themes and validate with domain knowledge (3 hrs)
If mitigation extraction is in scope: regex + LLM pipeline for mitigation conditions (6 hrs)
Synthesize findings into actionable recommendations (3 hrs)





Difficulty: MODERATE (time-consuming but well-scoped)

Deliverable 2 (Significant Impact) is the highest risk. It’s fundamentally a reading comprehension task on messy, agency-specific document formats. This is the one most likely to require an enterprise LLM, exceed its hour budget, AND still produce accuracy below expectations. I would flag this to the client as requiring a scoping conversation about acceptable accuracy levels.
The $750 LLM budget is probably too low. If Deliverable 2 requires GPT-4o-class models rather than mini models, and if prefiltering is less effective than assumed (messy text -> noisier filtering), the real LLM cost could be $1,000-2,000. The $500-1,000 range mentioned in the proposal is more realistic as a floor.
Timeline initiation remains a structural bottleneck. Deliverables 3 and 4 both depend on having good duration data, which requires good initiation dates. At 16% coverage, duration statistics are based on a small, potentially biased subset. The Federal Register NOI cross-referencing is the most promising path to improving this, but fuzzy matching introduces its own error rate.
The 180-200 hour estimate could easily become 250-300. Phase 1 taught that extraction from unstructured NEPA documents takes 2-3x longer than expected. The proposal’s internal breakdown sums to 190 hours, which assumes first-pass success on most deliverables. Budget a 30-50% overrun buffer.
Scope creep from “case study” and “outlier investigation” tasks. The timeline deliverable mentions investigating outliers through case studies – this is open-ended work that can expand indefinitely. Scope it tightly.





The concern about needing enterprise-level LLMs is well-founded, particularly for Deliverable 2. The Phase 1 experience with local Llama 3.2 3B showed that it works for classification (decision/initiation/other) but struggles with nuanced comprehension. Deliverable 2 (significance determinations) and to a lesser extent Deliverable 1 (NEPA triggers in ambiguous cases) are comprehension tasks, not classification tasks. The good news is that the rest of the infrastructure – regex prefiltering, BERT for scale, Quarto reporting, the combined datasets – transfers directly.
Recommendation: be transparent with the client that 190 hours is an optimistic estimate and that Deliverable 2 carries the highest technical risk of any Phase 2 deliverable. If the budget is firm, consider scoping Deliverable 2 as “exploratory” rather than “comprehensive” – e.g., focus on the top 3-4 agencies with the most standardized EIS formats rather than trying to cover all 60.

title: Phase 2 Deliverable Assessment
text:
Deliverable 2 (Significant Impact) is the highest risk. It’s fundamentally a reading comprehension task on messy, agency-specific document formats. This is the one most likely to require an enterprise LLM, exceed its hour budget, AND still produce accuracy below expectations. I would flag this to the client as requiring a scoping conversation about acceptable accuracy levels.
The $750 LLM budget is probably too low. If Deliverable 2 requires GPT-4o-class models rather than mini models, and if prefiltering is less effective than assumed (messy text -> noisier filtering), the real LLM cost could be $1,000-2,000. The $500-1,000 range mentioned in the proposal is more realistic as a floor.
Timeline initiation remains a structural bottleneck. Deliverables 3 and 4 both depend on having good duration data, which requires good initiation dates. At 16% coverage, duration statistics are based on a small, potentially biased subset. The Federal Register NOI cross-referencing is the most promising path to improving this, but fuzzy matching introduces its own error rate.
The 180-200 hour estimate could easily become 250-300. Phase 1 taught that extraction from unstructured NEPA documents takes 2-3x longer than expected. The proposal’s internal breakdown sums to 190 hours, which assumes first-pass success on most deliverables. Budget a 30-50% overrun buffer.
Scope creep from “case study” and “outlier investigation” tasks. The timeline deliverable mentions investigating outliers through case studies – this is open-ended work that can expand indefinitely. Scope it tightly.

title: Phase 2 Deliverable Assessment
text:
The concern about needing enterprise-level LLMs is well-founded, particularly for Deliverable 2. The Phase 1 experience with local Llama 3.2 3B showed that it works for classification (decision/initiation/other) but struggles with nuanced comprehension. Deliverable 2 (significance determinations) and to a lesser extent Deliverable 1 (NEPA triggers in ambiguous cases) are comprehension tasks, not classification tasks. The good news is that the rest of the infrastructure – regex prefiltering, BERT for scale, Quarto reporting, the combined datasets – transfers directly.
Recommendation: be transparent with the client that 190 hours is an optimistic estimate and that Deliverable 2 carries the highest technical risk of any Phase 2 deliverable. If the budget is firm, consider scoping Deliverable 2 as “exploratory” rather than “comprehensive” – e.g., focus on the top 3-4 agencies with the most standardized EIS formats rather than trying to cover all 60.

title: Phase 2, Deliverable 1: NEPA Triggered
text:
Last updated: 2026-02-11 POC script: code/phase2/deliverable01/poc_nepa_triggered.R



Classify why NEPA was triggered for each clean energy project — i.e., what is the federal government’s connection to the project (the “federal nexus”)?




NEPA only applies when the federal government is involved. The “federal nexus” is the specific connection. There are four categories:


The project is on federally owned or managed land. Trigger for most BLM, Forest Service, Bureau of Reclamation, NPS, and BIA projects. Examples: solar farm on BLM desert, transmission line crossing National Forest, wind farm on a military installation.



The project receives federal money — grants, loans, loan guarantees, Recovery Act/ARRA funds. Dominant trigger for DOE projects. DOE doesn’t own the project; NEPA applies to DOE’s decision to fund.



The project needs a specific federal permit, even if it’s on private land with private funding. Key permit types:

Right-of-way (ROW) across federal land (BLM)
Section 404 permit for wetland dredge/fill (Corps of Engineers)
Incidental take permit for endangered species (FWS)
FERC license for hydropower, natural gas pipelines
NRC license for nuclear facilities
Offshore lease from BOEM (offshore wind)




The federal agency is the project proponent — not funding or permitting someone else but doing it directly. Examples: BPA upgrading its own transmission lines, TVA building a power plant, WAPA replacing equipment.
These categories are not mutually exclusive. A transmission line on BLM land that crosses a wetland has both a Federal Land trigger and a Federal Permit (Section 404) trigger.







Two layers tested:

Metadata heuristic — map lead_agency to likely trigger category
Regex on project_description — search for explicit trigger language

The agency heuristic works extremely well for coverage — but 80.7% of all clean energy projects map to a single bucket: “Federal Funding / Action” under DOE. This is the central challenge for the deliverable.


DOE is the lead agency for 16,716 clean energy projects. But DOE’s involvement takes several distinct forms:

DOE grants — DOE provides a direct grant to a university, company, or state agency for clean energy R&D, demonstration, or deployment. This is the most common pattern.
DOE loan guarantees — DOE’s Loan Programs Office guarantees a loan for a large-scale project (e.g., a utility-scale solar farm). The private sector builds and owns the project.
Recovery Act (ARRA) funding — A specific funding mechanism from 2009-2012 that channeled billions through DOE for clean energy. Many CEs in the dataset are ARRA-funded.
DOE as direct actor — DOE itself undertakes the action on DOE-owned facilities (national labs, production sites). Here the nexus is federal action, not funding.
Power Marketing Administrations — BPA, WAPA, SWPA, SEPA are DOE sub-agencies that operate federal transmission systems. Their trigger is federal action (they own and operate the infrastructure), but they’re classified under DOE in the data.




Of the 16,716 DOE projects, the description regex found explicit trigger language in ~2,500 (15%): - “federal fund/grant/loan guarantee” → confirms funding as trigger - “Recovery Act” / “ARRA” → confirms specific funding mechanism - “right-of-way” / “federal land” → some DOE projects are actually on federal land (national lab sites)
The remaining ~14,000 DOE projects have descriptions but no explicit trigger language — they describe the project action without stating why DOE is involved. For most of these, the trigger is implicitly funding (DOE is providing the money), but the description just says things like “DOE proposes to provide technical assistance to…” or “Description of the Proposed Action: Install solar panels at…”



To break DOE into meaningful sub-categories:

Regex on descriptions (already partially working at 15%) — expand patterns to catch more funding language, loan program references, lab site names, ARRA identifiers
Sub-agency parsing — extract the specific DOE office from lead_agency (e.g., “Department of Energy - Energy Programs” vs. “Department of Energy - National Nuclear Security Administration”). The sub-agency often implies the trigger type.
CE category codes — DOE categorical exclusions have specific category codes (e.g., B5.1, B5.15) embedded in descriptions. These codes map to specific action types and could help distinguish funding-triggered CEs from action-triggered ones.
LLM for ambiguous cases — for the remaining projects where regex and sub-agency parsing don’t resolve the trigger type, an LLM pass on the first 1-2 pages of the project document could classify the federal nexus.

The good news: even if DOE disaggregation is imperfect, the broad trigger category (federal funding/action) is correct for all 16,716 projects. The question is how granular the client needs the breakdown to be.





This deliverable is feasible. The agency heuristic provides 99.1% broad-category coverage with zero document reading. The description regex adds specificity for 31% of projects. Only 142 projects (0.7%) have no signal at all.
The primary challenge is not whether we can identify the trigger, but how granular we can get — particularly within the DOE bucket. This should be scoped with the client: do they need “Federal Funding” vs. “Federal Action” within DOE, or is “Federal Funding / Action” sufficient?


Given the POC results, the original 35-50 hour estimate can likely be tightened: - If broad categories are sufficient: 20-25 hours - If DOE disaggregation is needed: 30-40 hours - LLM is likely only needed for validation and the 142 gap projects, not at scale





The four categories in the POC (Federal Land, Federal Funding, Federal Permit, Federal Action) are the standard textbook triggers, but there are additional or edge-case triggers worth accounting for:



Federal property disposal/transfer — When the government sells, transfers, or surpluses federal property or facilities. Distinct from “federal land” (which implies ongoing management). DOE site decommissioning, military base closures. Some DOE national lab projects may fall here.
Federal trust responsibility — For tribal lands, the federal government (via BIA) has a trust obligation. The land isn’t “federal land” in the BLM sense, but the trust relationship triggers NEPA. The 19 BIA projects in the data likely fall here. Currently lumped under “Federal Land / Trust” in the POC — should be its own category.
Federal management/planning decisions — Agency-wide resource management plans, programmatic decisions (BLM Resource Management Plans, Forest Plans). These are “federal actions” but programmatic, not project-specific. Some EIS projects in the dataset may be these.





Federal tax credits do NOT trigger NEPA. This matters for clean energy context: most private solar and wind projects receive ITC or PTC tax credits, but these aren’t considered “federal funding” under NEPA. The clean energy projects in NEPATEC have NEPA reviews because of some other nexus — federal land, a federal permit, or a direct DOE grant on top of the tax credit. This is a useful analytical point: the dataset captures clean energy projects with a direct federal nexus, not the full universe of clean energy projects.





Federal regulatory consultation — Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act requires federal agencies to consult with FWS/NMFS when actions may affect listed species. This can trigger or be folded into a NEPA review. In the data this shows up as FWS being lead agency, already mapped to “Federal Permit” in the POC.




Add “Federal Property Disposal/Transfer” as a fifth category. Keep “Federal Trust” separate from “Federal Land.” Note the tax credit exclusion in the analysis narrative to contextualize what the dataset does and doesn’t capture.
